items.stem: Evaluate Fagen et al.’s (2014) study of elephant learning in terms of one strength and one weakness.
items.answer: Strength (ethics): Positive reinforcement with food rewards replaced traditional training that relies on punishment, so the elephants were trained without fear or pain, improving their welfare. items.stem: Describe how the elephants in Fagen et al.’s study were trained.
items.answer: Mahouts used positive reinforcement: a bridging signal marked each correct response and food rewards followed; the trunk wash was broken into steps (target the trunk upwards, accept saline, hold, then lower and blow into a bag) and each step was shaped in sessions over several weeks.

items.stem: Evaluate Fagen et al.’s (2014) study of elephant learning, including a discussion of generalisability.
items.answer: Strength (ecological validity): Training took place in the elephants’ normal environment with their own mahouts, so the behaviour was learned in real working conditions. Strength (usefulness): The trunk wash allows elephants to be tested for tuberculosis safely, and the method shows mahouts an effective, humane alternative to traditional training. Weakness (generalisability): Only five young elephants from one centre in Nepal were trained, so the results may not apply to older elephants or other species. Weakness (controls): There was no control group trained with traditional methods, so we cannot be sure positive reinforcement was more effective than other methods. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.

items.answer: Arguments for: Fagen et al. trained young elephants to perform a complex trunk wash using shaping and positive reinforcement. items.answer: (a) The praise only condition had a higher mean (30.1) than the food rewards condition (24.0), suggesting that food rewards lead to faster learning than praise alone. (d) Repeated measures removes participant variables because the same people do both conditions, but order effects (practice or fatigue) and demand characteristics become more likely; counterbalancing would be needed.

items.markingKey: Positive reinforcement: increasing a behaviour by adding something pleasant after it. 1 mark for a partial definition; 2 marks for a full, accurate definition [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain one way Fagen et al.’s study can be applied to captive animal welfare. (b) Explain why the small sample in Fagen et al.’s study is a weakness.
items.answer: (a) Zoos and sanctuaries can use positive reinforcement to train animals to cooperate with health checks (such as trunk washes or blood samples), reducing stress and the need for restraint. (b) With only five young elephants, individual temperament strongly affects results, so we cannot be sure the method works for older elephants or all individuals.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark application; 1 mark welfare benefit [2] (b) 1 mark small; 1 mark consequence [2]

items.stem: Outline one strength and one weakness of Fagen et al.’s (2014) study of elephant learning, with one point about generalisability.
items.answer: Strength (usefulness): The trunk wash allows elephants to be tested for tuberculosis safely, and the method shows mahouts an effective, humane alternative to traditional training. Weakness (generalisability): Only five young elephants from one centre in Nepal were trained, so the results may not apply to older elephants or other species.
items.markingKey: 2 marks for each point: 1 mark identification, 1 mark explanation in the context of the study [4]

items.stem: A zoo in Lagos needs to take regular blood samples from its giraffes, which currently have to be restrained. Explain one welfare benefit of this approach.
items.answer: Animals cooperate voluntarily, so they are less stressed than when restrained and injuries are less likely.
items.markingKey: 1 mark benefit; 1 mark explained [2]

items.stem: An elephant centre near Auckland compared the number of training sessions needed to learn a trunk wash for 8 elephants trained with food rewards and 8 elephants trained with verbal praise only. Table: Training sessions needed — Food rewards: 27, 26, 23, 12, 31, 25, 29, 24. Praise only: 34, 39, 28, 38, 41, 45, 41, 37. Using the mean scores, state one conclusion that can be drawn from these results.
items.answer: The praise only condition had a higher mean (37.9) than the food rewards condition (24.6), suggesting that food rewards lead to faster learning than praise alone.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: conclusion about the effect of the IV on the DV; 1 mark: supported with the means [2]

items.stem: A zoo in Cairo needs to take regular blood samples from its giraffes, which currently have to be restrained. (a) Use Fagen et al.’s study to suggest how keepers could train the giraffes. (b) Explain one welfare benefit of this approach.
items.answer: (a) Use shaping with positive reinforcement: reward the giraffe for standing at a station, then for allowing touch on the neck, then for a small needle, using a bridge and food rewards. (b) Animals cooperate voluntarily, so they are less stressed than when restrained and injuries are less likely.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark shaping; 1 mark reinforcement detail [2] (b) 1 mark benefit; 1 mark explained [2]

items.stem: ‘Operant conditioning is the most effective way of training animals.’ Discuss this view. In your answer, you may refer to animal welfare and shaping.
items.answer: Arguments for: Fagen et al. trained young elephants to perform a complex trunk wash using shaping and positive reinforcement. Reinforcement-based training is humane and builds cooperation. Arguments against: Not every animal learned the full behaviour, so individual differences matter. There was no comparison with other methods. Some behaviours may be learned by observation or be partly innate. Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: accurate, detailed psychological knowledge (named studies/theories) used to build a two-sided argument; evaluation includes issues such as validity, reliability, generalisability, ethics or usefulness; a justified conclusion. Middle band: relevant knowledge with some evaluation, but one side or the conclusion is underdeveloped. Lower band: limited, mostly descriptive answer with little evaluation.

items.stem: Which term describes the following: “Increasing a behaviour by removing something unpleasant after it”?
items.answer: Negative reinforcement
items.markingKey: Negative reinforcement: increasing a behaviour by removing something unpleasant after it. [1]

items.stem: Fagen et al.’s (2014) study of elephant learning can be evaluated in terms of usefulness. Explain one strength of the study relating to this issue.
items.answer: The trunk wash allows elephants to be tested for tuberculosis safely, and the method shows mahouts an effective, humane alternative to traditional training.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies a relevant strength linked to usefulness; 1 mark: explained using detail from the study [2]

items.stem: Explain why shaping is needed to train a complex behaviour such as a trunk wash.
items.answer: An animal is unlikely to perform the whole behaviour by chance, so each step (lifting the trunk, holding liquid, blowing into a bag) is reinforced in turn until the full sequence is produced.
items.markingKey: 1 mark complex behaviour unlikely spontaneously; 1 mark steps reinforced [2]

items.stem: An elephant centre near Kuala Lumpur compared the number of training sessions needed to learn a trunk wash for 8 elephants trained with food rewards and 8 elephants trained with verbal praise only. Table: Training sessions needed — Food rewards: 22, 21, 29, 15, 28, 21, 20, 15. Praise only: 28, 27, 31, 26, 32, 36, 27, 36. Calculate the median score for the food rewards condition.
items.markingKey: Ordered scores: 15, 15, 20, 21, 21, 22, 28, 29; median = 21. 1 mark: data ordered; 1 mark: correct median [2]

items.stem: Evaluate Fagen et al.’s (2014) study of elephant learning, including a discussion of quantitative data.
items.answer: Strength (ecological validity): Training took place in the elephants’ normal environment with their own mahouts, so the behaviour was learned in real working conditions. Strength (quantitative data): Progress was recorded as the number of sessions needed to reach each step, so learning could be compared across elephants. Weakness (controls): There was no control group trained with traditional methods, so we cannot be sure positive reinforcement was more effective than other methods. Weakness (reliability): Each elephant had a different mahout and individual temperament, so the procedure was not identical for all animals and may be hard to replicate exactly. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: strengths and weaknesses are accurate, well explained and clearly linked to the study, the named issue is discussed, the answer is well organised and reaches a conclusion. Middle band: points are mostly accurate but one side is less developed or links to the study are general. Lower band: points are identified but brief, generic or one-sided. Description of the procedure without evaluation receives little credit.

items.stem: Who carried out the day-to-day training of the elephants?
options: Their mahouts (handlers), guided by the researchers
items.answer: Their mahouts (handlers), guided by the researchers
items.markingKey: Mahouts were taught positive reinforcement techniques. [1]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Describe how the elephants in Fagen et al.’s study were trained. (b) In a revision session, a student says: “Fagen et al.’s study can be described as a series of case studies of individual elephants.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Mahouts used positive reinforcement: a bridging signal marked each correct response and food rewards followed; the trunk wash was broken into steps (target the trunk upwards, accept saline, hold, then lower and blow into a bag) and each step was shaped in sessions over several weeks. (b) Correct. Each elephant’s progress was tracked separately.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark positive reinforcement/food; 1 mark bridge; 1 mark shaping steps [3] (b) 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: With reference to Fagen et al.’s (2014) study of elephant learning, explain one strength relating to quantitative data.
items.answer: Progress was recorded as the number of sessions needed to reach each step, so learning could be compared across elephants.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies a relevant strength linked to quantitative data; 1 mark: explained using detail from the study [2]

items.stem: Nadia recorded correct and incorrect attempts for each elephant during the last week of training. Elephant B: correct 13, incorrect 4; Elephant E: correct 16, incorrect 8. Calculate the percentage of attempts for Elephant B that were “correct”. Give your answer to one decimal place.

An elephant centre near Dubai compared the number of training sessions needed to learn a trunk wash for 6 elephants trained with food rewards and 6 elephants trained with verbal praise only. items.answer: Food rewards: 14; praise only: 8.

items.stem: A researcher in Lagos is interested in whether dogs learn a new trick faster with food rewards or with praise. Plan a field experiment to test this. Your plan must include: ethical issues, how the dependent variable will be measured and the sampling technique.
items.answer: Method: a field experiment. Manipulate the IV in a natural everyday setting; participants may not know they are being studied; standardise as much of the procedure as possible. Variables: IV: food rewards or praise; DV: number of trials to learn the trick. Sample: for example an opportunity or volunteer sample of about 30 people from the target population in Lagos, with reasons. Design/procedure: clear, replicable steps, with standardised instructions and random allocation or counterbalancing where relevant. Ethics: informed consent, right to withdraw, protection from harm, confidentiality and a full debrief. Data: quantitative scores summarised with means and a suitable graph; qualitative answers analysed into themes where collected.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: a detailed, accurate and replicable plan using the stated method; all required features are included and are appropriate to the aim; variables are operationalised; ethics are addressed. Middle band: a workable plan with most required features but some lack detail or are not justified. Lower band: a basic plan with few features or with errors in method.

items.stem: A researcher in Manila is interested in how zoo visitors’ behaviour affects animals in an enclosure. Plan an observation to test this. Your plan must include: how inter-rater reliability will be checked, behavioural categories, the type of observation and the sampling technique. Then explain one weakness of your plan and how it could be overcome.
items.answer: Method: an observation. Structured observation with operationalised behavioural categories and time sampling; two observers to check inter-rater reliability; overt or covert as appropriate. Variables: behaviour: animal responses; categories: approaching, hiding, pacing. Sample: for example an opportunity or volunteer sample of about 30 people from the target population in Manila, with reasons. Design/procedure: clear, replicable steps, with standardised instructions and random allocation or counterbalancing where relevant. Ethics: informed consent, right to withdraw, protection from harm, confidentiality and a full debrief. Data: quantitative scores summarised with means and a suitable graph; qualitative answers analysed into themes where collected. Weakness: for example a small or biased sample; overcome by a larger, more representative sample.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: a detailed, accurate and replicable plan using the stated method; all required features are included and are appropriate to the aim; variables are operationalised; ethics are addressed. Middle band: a workable plan with most required features but some lack detail or are not justified. Lower band: a basic plan with few features or with errors in method.
